subject: Anatomy
summary: The elbow is a hinge joint formed by the humerus, radius, and ulna, stabilized by ligaments and muscles. It allows flexion, extension, pronation, and supination, essential for hand positioning.

sections.p: The elbow is a complex hinge joint that connects the arm to the forearm, enabling a range of movements vital for daily tasks.
The joint is located between the distal humerus and the proximal radius and ulna. The trochlea, capitulum, radial head, and olecranon form the articular surfaces.
Adjacent structures include the brachial artery and median nerve medially, and the radial nerve laterally. The ulnar nerve runs posterior to the medial epicondyle.
b: Brachial artery runs medial to joint
Median nerve passes between pronator teres and flexor digitorum
Radial nerve courses lateral to lateral epicondyle

sections.p: The elbow receives arterial input from the brachial artery and its branches: the superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries.
Motor innervation is via the radial, median, and ulnar nerves, while sensory input comes from the median and ulnar nerves.
Primary movements are flexion and extension; secondary movements include pronation/supination and small rotational adjustments.
Common injuries include fractures of the olecranon, radial head, and distal humerus, as well as ligamentous sprains and nerve compressions.
b: Olecranon fracture: posterior pain, inability to extend

t.b: Assesses soft tissue injuries; useful if ligament damage suspected
Evaluates nerve function when compression is suspected

sections.p: Remember the 'rule of the elbow': pain with flexion indicates ulnar nerve irritation; pain with extension suggests radial nerve irritation.
b: Check for 'Tinel's sign' over cubital tunnel

sections.p: Treat fractures with immobilization or surgery; ligamentous injuries often require rest and physiotherapy; nerve compressions may need decompression.

t.b: Controls pain; NSAIDs preferred unless contraindicated
Reduce inflammation in severe ligamentous injury

sections.p: Distinguish from wrist injuries and shoulder dislocations by assessing range of motion and pain location.
b: Wrist fracture: pain distal to elbow

sections.p: X‑ray may miss subtle fractures; EMG can be falsely normal early in nerve injury.
b: Early EMG: may not show changes until 3-4 weeks

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pain with inability to move, deformity, neurovascular deficit, open wounds, or signs of infection (fever, redness, swelling).

faq.q: What is the most common elbow fracture in children?
faq.a: The supracondylar fracture of the humerus, often from a fall on an outstretched hand.

faq.q: How do you differentiate a medial epicondyle fracture from a simple sprain?
faq.a: A displaced medial epicondyle fracture shows a visible bump and loss of flexion strength; a sprain does not.

faq.q: Why is the ulnar nerve at risk during elbow surgery?
faq.a: It runs posterior to the medial epicondyle and can be stretched or compressed by surgical hardware.

exam: Explain the stabilizing structures of the elbow joint and their roles in preventing dislocation.
Describe the clinical approach to a patient with suspected olecranon fracture, including history, examination, and investigations.
Outline the management plan for a patient with a supracondylar humeral fracture in a low‑resource setting.
